utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis for the Prosecution assisted today by our intern, Jaspreet Saini, and our case manager, Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And could we have the appearances for the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel, Stefane Bourgon, co-counsel, and Muriel Cauvin, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present, members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else in the courtroom. And I wouldn't want to forget those who are around the courtroom as well and who are contributing to the smooth running of the proceedings. Today we will be continuing with the examination of a witness who was testifying a couple of days ago. There was no hearing yesterday. Without wasting any more time, I will ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. Your examination will now continue after the break that we had yesterday, which allowed you to have a rest. I will now ask -- or rather, I'll now give the floor to Defence counsel so that they can continue with their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. Mr. President, could the General be shown the series of documents entitled Dusina and Miletici, so that I can continue with my examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, if you remember, towards the end of the hearing on Tuesday, we were discussing the events that took place when Colonel Blaskic informed you that it was suspected that individuals had been killed in Dusina. My last question had to do with the fact that the meeting on UNPROFOR premises was continued on the following day, and you then said that you provided the information that you had gathered the previous day. Do you remember that, General?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now have a look at documents under number 31, the document number is 0664, and I will ask my colleague, Mr. Bourgon, to read out the first sentence in item 5 -- in item 9 so that I can ask you some questions. I apologise, Mr. President, but my English is such that it would be better for Mr. Bourgon to read those two sentences out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 5 in document 0664. [In English] Very detailed report on the alleged assassination of the HVO delegation. His conclusion was that the HVO delegation was not travelling in order to arrange prisoner exchange and that they were killed in an area where fighting was going on between the HVO and BiH army. BiH forces were on high alert because of the fighting during the day."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, does this part of the ECMM report reflect what you were just saying? You provide a report on what you had found out about the previous day.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, in the course of that day, was an agreement on a cease-fire signed?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the 27th of January, 1993. That's the date when an agreement on a cease-fire was signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, tell me: In the course of that day, during the break or during the meeting or the break, did HVO representatives make another complaint?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Do you know whether this complaint was verified; if so, by whom, and what were the results of the verification?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember who verified the allegations made by the HVO, nor do I know what the results of this verification were. I wasn't -- I didn't have the opportunity of verifying this, because I didn't have the necessary links with my superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will now ask my colleague to read out the following item: Item number 9 in this ECMM report. And I will then put my question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 9 in document 0664. [In English]: "During the break, the negotiations were put at risk by the HVO allegation of the burning and shelling of Busovaca from Fojnica. Quick verification of the rumours with the UN forces in those villages proved that they were totally unfounded. The HVO agreed on continuing the negotiations."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, if you go back to that meeting now, could you tell us whether, after this complaint had been dealt with, the meeting continued, and only then was the agreement signed.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there was a break that we had, that I didn't know that the UN verified the HVO allegations. I know that discussions continued and very soon the agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, after the agreement had been signed, was a Busovaca commission ever formed, the one that you have already mentioned? And when was its first meeting held?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember when the Busovaca joint commission had its first meeting. I mentioned the composition of the Busovaca joint commission, but I do remember that a few days later, after the agreement on the cease-fire in Kiseljak had been signed, the work of the Busovaca joint commission commenced.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the information that you obtained and the investigation launched in Zenica, and in addition to the fact that you provided a report at the meeting, at that time, did the Croatian television, the media and the HVO carry news, relay news, that had no basis when you verified the allegations?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was staying in the territory of Busovaca, I was able to follow television footage. I can't remember whether this was a local TV channel or whether it was the Croatian radio/television channel, but what was depicted did not reflect the information I had obtained through reports while I was staying in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, when looking at the documents issued by the 3rd Corps with regard to the Lasva junction, we could see that a company was re-subordinated to the municipal staff in order to secure that area. Tell me, please: Since you have already spoken about how difficult it was to establish the unit planned, tell me, how many men were there in one company?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the kind of company, but between 100 and 120 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, at that time, in January, in those operations in that combat in Dusina, was there a member of the Supreme Command Staff who was in charge, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm sure that not a single member of the Supreme Command Staff was in command. These units were very small, so such a high-level person wouldn't have been in command of such units and of such an operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If certain documents made such allegations, what would your comment be?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't believe that that's something that could happen in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, when checking up your information, the combat operations, state of the army in that area, were you in some other way informed of the fact that the Mujahedin had been involved in certain activities in the Dusina area?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, could you now have a look at document number 23, please. It's a document from the command of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, from the HVO. And first of all, could you tell me if you know who Vehbij Keric is?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mr. Vehbij Keric. He was a member of the Supreme Command Staff, with its headquarters in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you have a look at the second paragraph, have a look at the last sentence, or the last part of the last sentence, would it be correct to say that it says that Vehbij Keric is in command of all operations, as well as Enver Hadzihasanovic, and the main objective of the operations is the full elimination of the HVO in the Central Bosnian Operation Zone? Is this claim totally false or is this something that you were aware of at the time?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is completely false. This statement is completely false, and I don't understand how something like this could be written.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please have a look at P628. It's under number 24. Naturally, I'm not showing you all the other contents of the previous document, but I wanted to draw your attention to some of the falsehoods contained in that document. This document, under number 24, is also a report from the HVO. The exhibit number is P644. In the last two sentences in this document, they mention that in -- that Zvonko Rajic went to negotiate, and in the course of the negotiations, our members were killed, which shows what the character of the aggressor is. Afterwards, Lasva and Dusina were burnt down. Nothing is known about the fate of the population. If you can remember everything that you established on that day and during those days, can you say whether these allegations that there were some negotiations during which these people were killed, could you say whether any facts confirmed the allegations contained in this document?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the report, I didn't find out that there were any negotiations, but the reports did show that HVO members were not brutally killed, and they showed that Dusina was not set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at P723 now. It's under number 27. P723. In this document from the HVO, dated the 27th of January, under A, the Muslim forces, in the third paragraph, again it states that these forces were personally commanded by Vehbij Keric and Enver Hadzihasanovic. Do you stand by what you just said, that Vehbij Keric, a member of the Supreme Command Staff, has nothing to do with this, or rather, I don't want to put words into your mouth, but tell me whether Vehbij Keric was there and whether he personally commanded this operation.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I myself know, Vehbij Keric was not in that area at the time, and I stand by what I have already said. In the case of such a small-scale operation, such a high-level member of the BH army wouldn't have been in command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The first paragraph of the report, it says, and this is the third line, it says that the main forces of the 3rd Corps of the Muslim forces from Zenica were used, around 8.500 soldiers strong. What would you say about this statement?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, we didn't have such strong forces. This is a really very significant force mentioned here, and at the time in Zenica we didn't have such forces that were organised and ready for combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, could we now have a look at the second part of these documents, under number 16 there is a document I would like to have a look at. P649, dated the 25th of January, 1993. Can you see the document? It's addressed to the government of the Republic of Croatia to Hrvoje Sarinic, personally. It's under number 16.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document I have is in English. I don't understand English.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the pages that follow. Perhaps you have the B/C/S version that follows the English one.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The B/C/S version is at the end. Please put your question to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you read out the last two sentences in the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the mixed village of Dusina. Is that the sentence you are referring to? "In the mixed village of Dusina, all the Croatian houses were set on fire, and women, children, and elderly are being subjected to a downright slaughter. We still have no accurate information about the casualties there, but we do know that 33 HVO soldiers were killed. The brutality of the Muslim forces is proven by the fact that all seven members of the HVO delegation that had been negotiating with the BH army were killed tonight."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, you've already told us about what you found out and what you reported, and we have now had a look at a number of official HVO documents. As far as what has just been read out, were these rumours that were repeated and relayed via the media in Central Bosnia, or rather, by the Croatian television?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would be correct to say that the Croatian television depicted the events in a way that had nothing to do with the situation in the field, and the last document I have read is dated the 25th of January, 1993. And at that time, there was no combat in the village of Dusina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the sort of news that was carried during that period of time, tell me whether the Busovaca commission decided to go into the field to verify these allegations; and if that was the case, can you tell me what you know about this?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Croatian television and the local television of the HVO, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I made a complaint at the joint commission. I said that this did not correspond to the truth. Afterwards, it was decided to visit that area and establish what the actual situation was in the village of Dusina. A few days after the events in the village of Dusina, representatives of the Busovaca joint commission went to the area of Dusina to see what the situation there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was this commission composed of?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were representatives of the European Monitoring Mission, UNPROFOR representatives, and other representatives of international organisations, I think. On behalf of the HVO, there was Mr. Franjo Nakic. On behalf of the BH army, I myself represented the BH army, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, did you visit the village of Dusina, and did you determine that the entire village had been set on fire?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The joint commission visited the village of Dusina and the village hadn't been set on fire. There were traces of combat, though. I do remember very well that the translator in the joint commission was someone called Milica Kegelj. She asked us to visit her relatives' house. I remember entering her relatives' house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you meet any local inhabitants or BH army members in the area?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: While passing through the village, we saw that there were inhabitants and members of the BH army there. I remember speaking to a local commander. I can't remember his name. We asked him to tell us what had happened, and he told us that there had been armed combat in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did any of the inhabitants you spoke to mention any individuals being killed?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, none of the inhabitants said anything about anyone being killed in Dusina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at document number 39 now, P222. It's from the HVO. Have a look at the second page to see who signed it, and is this the person who went to visit the area, to inspect the site?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that this is Mr. Franjo Nakic's signature, but the person who was with me on that day and at that time in Dusina was someone called Franjo Nakic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document from the HVO which refers to a meeting of your commission. Pay attention to what Mr. Fleming said. Have a look at what Mr. Fleming said. It says that Mr. Fleming said very positive things about the army and in the last line it says that the place, Busovaca, which we visited is in a sorry state. The inhabitants are afraid and desperate. And for Lasva and Dusina, he says it was difficult to avoid the impression that something terrible had happened. But the citizens who were there either didn't say anything or were afraid to say something. Does this confirm the fact that the citizens didn't say anything, apart from the fact that they heard from commander that there had been fighting there? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since Nakic was also there, he did not have any suggestions with regard to these developments. He thought that everything was clear. Was that Nakic's position or was he still insisting that something should be done on the part of the Busovaca commission?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember only too well that when it came to Dusina, Mr. Nakic did not have any issues to raise with this regard. However, when it came to the joint commission and its works and other incidents that had taken place in Busovaca and the following days that ensued, Mr. Nakic did have issues to raise, I had issues to raise, and this is what we had to deal with, with the problems that we encountered in the territory of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It stems from this document that European monitors were also there. Were there members of the Busovaca commission or was it UNPROFOR, as you have just told us a while ago?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You may not have understood me when I said that members of the European Monitoring Mission were there. They were the ones involved in the joint commission. There were also members of UNPROFOR, and I also said that I don't remember which other international organisations were represented. But in any case, there was the European Mission and UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, General: Since you spoke with the villagers, since you asked them what had happened, did the representative of the army, when mentioning fighting, hint to the fact that there might have been killings during the fighting, or alternatively, wasn't there any such information?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the information that I had and reports that I could see, I could conclude that there had been combat and that there were casualties on both sides. This is what I could learn from the reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were there, did you receive any other information that might have changed the opinion that you based on the reports?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Everything was exactly as the reports depicted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at document number 40. This is a 3rd Corps document. Once the cease-fire agreement was signed and once the agreement was reached, did the command of the 3rd Corps issue an order with regard to this cease-fire, and did he issue very clear orders based on the Geneva Conventions and treatment of property and the civilian population? Can you look at page 2. There is this order.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is precisely the order that you have described.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, you've told us that when you returned from the meeting, you learned about this investigation and that the civilian police was involved because they had better equipment. Did there come a time, General, when you learnt what the results of the investigation were? If you did, did they change your views on the developments in Dusina, based on the initial information?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any further insight into what happened subsequently. However, I did learn that the case had been taken over by the prosecutor's office, by the military prosecutor's office, and that in practical terms this case was under consideration. I did not have any further information. However, whatever information I had at the time confirmed the fact that there hadn't been a crime and that any casualties that took place were a result of combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In January and February, did the military police of the 3rd Corps, or the civilian police of the 3rd Corps - sorry - the civilian police of Zenica, were they able to go to Busovaca and Kiseljak and conduct interview with certain individuals?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of January and the beginning of February 1993, the entire territory of Busovaca and municipality was the theatre of combat, and the only means of transportation was UNPROFOR vehicles. That's the only way one could get to that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, in Kiseljak, Busovaca, and Vitez, when the HVO took complete control there, did the legal authorities have any means to perform their duties in those areas?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that in the municipalities with the majority Croatian population, the power of the Croatian Defence Council had already been established and legal authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina could not function there. To the contrary; their work was banned in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, you have told us that, in order to check all the reports and all the media news, you joined the commission and went to Dusina. Did Commander Hadzihasanovic also inform his superior command about the news that was aired in the media?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that my commander did that. I am sure that he informed his superior command of what was going on in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at document under number 34. This is a report that the 3rd Corps sent to the Supreme Command Staff. Can you please look at items 11, 12, and 13. Would this be the response of the commander to the information in the media and the allegations that the negotiators had been killed and the villages had been burnt, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now one more thing about Dusina. Let's go back to the fact that you have just mentioned, and that is that the legal authorities could not perform their duties in the territories where the HVO had complete control. There were just HVO bodies in those areas. Do you know: These people who left Dusina, where they went?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they went. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there an exchange of prisoners from Dusina? Where did these people go, and where, and when?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, some of the population from Dusina went towards Zenica, and some went towards Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Croatian Defence Council have an opportunity in Dusina to talk to these people and learn about the events that had taken place in Dusina?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. Not in Dusina, but in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose they did have such an opportunity in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at document 42. This is P906. And can you please tell me who created this document, and when was it created? When was it issued?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was created by the prosecutor's office in Travnik, seated in Vitez. The number of this document is 593/95, and the date is 17 November 1995. It was addressed to the high court in Travnik, with its seat in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was in control in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian Defence Council was in control in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document was drafted almost three and a half years [as interpreted] after the developments in Dusina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to your information, did anything else happen, or were you informed of any other facts for which you would have changed your opinion that the casualties had taken place in combat? Did anybody tell you anything to the contrary in the course of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, during that period of time, nobody ever provided me with any new facts, with any new information that would make me change my mind. I adhered to the fact that I learnt that there had been combat activities in Dusina and, as a result of those combat activities, there were casualties on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, when you look back at those developments, could you tell me whether the 3rd Corps and its commander did everything possible to investigate, and did they endeavour to find out what had happened in Dusina after having received information from the enemy that there might have been a crime there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I sit here today, I can say with full responsibility that the corps command did their utmost and went even beyond that, because they established full cooperation with the civilian bodies and with all the professional bodies that could establish what had happened to those people who were killed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Can we now move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, before it disappears off the screen, I do believe there might be an error in the translation, at least in the English. At line 24, which is on the preceding page and is about to disappear, there's reference to document P906 being drafted three and a half years after the developments in Dusina, and I believe that might be an error, in light of the date of that document and the date of which the events in Dusina occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The date is 17 November 1995. This document that was drafted by the high public prosecutor's office in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is exactly what we're saying. This document was drafted two and a half years, almost three years later. This is an HVO document. But the final arguments, those who could have full information initiated investigation three years later -- actually, two years after the events. Two years would be January. Since this is November, it's almost three years after the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying, in line 9 of page 17, you are saying that this is an HVO document. This document is not marked as being an HVO document. This is something that was drafted by the high public prosecutor's office in Travnik. Unless in 1995 it was the HVO that controlled everything. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I did not want to say that. The witness said that in 1995, this area was under the control of the HVO, still; although the Washington Agreements had taken place earlier, still this was under the control of the HVO. At the same time, the legal court, the legal prosecutor's office were in Travnik. We heard Mr. Djeric here who worked in Travnik at the time. So this document shows that the party that had a full insight and all the possibilities to investigate the events failed to do that for three years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, let us move on to another issue. Did you, in your capacity as deputy commander or as a member of a joint commission, did you ever learn of a crime having been committed in Miletici?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received initial information as a member of the joint commission, which at the time was seated in Vitez. Again, this joint commission was composed of representatives of the European Monitoring Mission, representatives of the UNPROFOR, representatives of other international organisations who came on board from time to time, and it was Mr. Nakic on behalf of HVO, and I was representing the BiH army in that commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And who did the information come from?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Mr. Franjo Nakic, at one of the regular meetings of the joint commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did you decide to do, General, when you received that information?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was surprised that there was such information, and I wanted to go to the site, to Miletici, to see what had happened, to establish what the actual situation was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go there, and if you did, who was it who went there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On that day, which was 25 April 1993, if I remember well, we went to Miletici, the representatives of the joint commission from Vitez Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were the HVO and the army represented? What about the international community?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that there were both the HVO, the BiH army, and international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Miletici, what did you see there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were taken there by the personnel carriers, owned by BritBat. I had an opportunity to see what the situation many Miletici was, and I did see that people had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go somewhere from the village? And when you returned from the village, did you meet with somebody? Can you elaborate a little on that.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we returned, vehicles stopped. At that time, I did not have information where we were being driven. We were sitting in the personnel carrier, which didn't have any windows. Together with Mr. Franjo Nakic and the interpreter, we -- I got off. We saw some people rallied around us. We asked them who they were, and they told us that they were from Miletici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These people from Miletici, did they tell you what had happened on the previous day?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We spoke to these people, and we couldn't see who of them were Croats, who were Bosniaks. They were sort of mixed. And both Mr. Nakic and I spoke to them. What I managed to learn from the people, and Mr. Nakic was present there as well, was that these killings had been committed by some foreign members, and I believe that they referred to them as the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you told at the time what had happened, what had transpired?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They told us very briefly that the incident had occurred a day later, that a group of Mujahedin stormed into their village, that they were looking for arms, that they wanted to disarm the villagers, and that the entire village, both Croats as well as Muslims, were taken somewhere else. They could not tell us exactly where they were taken. They also told us that five members of the Croatian population had been singled out from the crowd, that these five had remained in the village. I believe that those are the same five people whom I saw dead in Miletici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody mention the fact that there might have been members of the BiH army among those Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, nobody among the villagers mentioned the presence of BiH army members who would be there with the foreigners.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that village where you spoke with the population, did you see any members of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to be very precise here. I did not speak to anybody in Miletici. There was nobody there. I spoke with these people not far from Miletici, a few kilometres away from Miletici, as we were returning from the village. In other words, I did not speak to anybody in the village itself. I spoke to the villagers outside the village, and I could see several members of the army among those villagers. I can't remember how many. Maybe three, four, or five. I can't remember exactly. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Among these three, four, or five members of the army, did you recognise anybody as being one of the commanders? And did you issue any orders to that person? Did you warn that person about anything, if that was the case?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were any commanders among them. I wanted to speak to the local commander, and one person responded. And I also told Mr. Nakic that the population could go back to Miletici and that we would guarantee their safety. And if my memory serves me well, I told the local commander that he had to secure the village and that he had to look after the Croatian population, because we, as the army, had to guarantee the safety of all the citizens, including the Croatian population. And I remember this very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, these Croats, where were they accommodated in the village where you stopped, and who looked after them?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I did not have any information at the time as to who looked after them and where they were accommodated. But I know that some of the Croatian population expressed a wish to go to Bila. At least, that is what Franjo Nakic told me at the time. I don't know, I can't remember where they were accommodated and who provided security for them. I didn't have that information at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your conversation that you and Mr. Franjo Nakic had with the international representatives, were there any doubts as to who had committed the crime?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think there were any doubts, for me or for Mr. Franjo Nakic. According to what the villagers had told us in Miletici, it was clear to us that foreigners called the Mujahedin had committed these murders.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps, were the foreigners linked to the BH army in any way?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I can say that there were no foreigners in the BH army, and in particular, there were no Mujahedin in the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, could you now have a look at these documents that are about the events in Miletici. Document number 1 is a BritBat document. On page 3 -- do you see it? Paragraph 3, and it says that the local Bosniak Croats [as interpreted] initially claimed that Muslim extremists had killed five Croats. The details are based on statements given by the inhabitants, collected by members of unit 912L. The inhabitants say that an unknown number of Muslim soldiers came to the village. The inhabitants wanted to say that these were extremists and not the regular troops of the BH army. This document mentions Muslim extremists. Tell me: Given what you spoke about with the inhabitants, was this the correct expression, or rather, would it be more correct to say that the Mujahedin had entered the village?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The inhabitants told us that the Mujahedin had entered the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at document number 2, please. It's an HVO document. P289. In the second sentence, in the first paragraph, this event is described. It says that the Mujahedin arrived in Miletici, in the morning, and gathered all of its inhabitants at gunpoint. Does this correspond to the information that you obtained, or is this something that the inhabitants didn't inform you about?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this report, it says that the Mujahedin committed the murders. This is what we found out from the inhabitants when we went to the place. So this is confirmed by -- this confirms what we found out at the site.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at document under number 3. This is an HVO document. It's from the Central Bosnia Operative Zone Command. It's Exhibit P416. In the second paragraph, there's a reference to the number of inhabitants taken away, 60 to 70 persons. In paragraph 3, it says that part of the group is in the building of the elementary school in Zagradje. And paragraph 4 refers to the source and it says that in the course of the night, the Mujahedin forces will be taking this group to Zenica through the forest. Is this the kind of information you found out from anyone in the field?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time that I see that this information is from the Central Bosnia Operative Zone Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at document under number 5. It's also a BritBat document. At the end of A, on the first page of the B/C/S version, it says that the bodies of five Bosnian Croats who were killed in the attack in Miletici were taken to the local cemetery by BritBat. Were you present at the time or did that take place a little later?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember all the details. I don't know whether the bodies of the men killed were transported on that day. But I saw that UNPROFOR members were carrying a body wrapped up in a blanket on that day. But as to whether they were taken to the local cemetery, I wasn't there and I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, this document is P375. Have a look at document 6, please. At the end of the B/C/S version, and the number is P576, in this daily report of the 27th of April, the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia provides additional information on the massacre in Miletici, and it says that the Mujahedin and local Muslims participated in the massacre. And then it mentions some names and it says that apparently Osman Tahirovic brought the Mujahedin to the village in a tractor, et cetera, et cetera. Did you have such information that people with these local names participated in murdering these individuals? Did you find out about such events from the inhabitants that you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'd just like to confirm what I heard on that day. The inhabitants we came across when returning from Miletici, who were of mixed ethnic composition, they said they were from Miletici. They were from Miletici and they were Croats and Muslims. And they said that the Mujahedin had committed the murders, both the Croatian and Muslim inhabitants of Miletici made this claim.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, after this event, were there various versions contained in various reports? Were the events you found out about from eyewitnesses on that day depicted in different ways, the events you found out about in the village of Miletici?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were very -- I know that rumours can be very negative, can cause a lot of problems. I know that rumours spread very rapidly. I'm not sure what sort of rumours there were about these events, but I have told you about what I saw and what I heard, what I was told by the inhabitants when returning from the village of Miletici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, since you were an eyewitness of the situation that remained unchanged after those inhabitants were killed, and as you said, it was obvious that those inhabitants had been killed, and you have repeated on several occasions that there was no doubt about the fact that the Mujahedin had committed these murders, tell me, General: Did the BH army feel obliged to investigate crimes committed by men who were not army members? Was that their obligation? And did the BH army have the possibility of investigating such individuals?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I should say that at that time, the military was not interested in Miletici. It wasn't a village that was interesting in military terms. It wasn't in the area of combat operations at the time. And given what I found out about -- given what the inhabitants told me at the site, I believed that it wasn't the 3rd Corps's duty to investigate that case, because I found out that BH army members weren't involved and these events didn't occur in a zone of combat operations. In military terms, Miletici was of no interest.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, which military units were present in that area, in the area of Miletici, in the area of Maline? Were they just units or brigades of the BH army there, or were there any other military units present in that area?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I know for sure that there were several military units in that area. There was a unit from the BH army. There was the 306th Brigade. There were HVO units. The HVO units were very near the village of Miletici. There was the civilian police, the regular civilian police force, the reserve civilian police force. They were all armed. They all carried weapons. There were UNPROFOR units, which were also armed. So there were various units in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And who were you responsible for, as far as disciplining is concerned, as far as punishing crimes is concerned?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already testified about this. It was the duty of the BH army to launch an investigation only if it came to light that BH army members had committed crimes. As I have already said, this area was outside the zone of responsibility and was of no interest in military terms. There was the civilian police there and the civilian authorities were present there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me whether you know that our units that were in that area, the 306th Brigade and other units, do you know whether they informed the 3rd Corps headquarters that, in the presence of the Mujahedin was a problem and that it wasn't possible for them to communicate with them?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say, but as far as I can remember right now, the command closest to the village of Miletici was the command of the 306th Mountain Brigade, and naturally, they were ordered to see what was happening. As far as I know, they didn't manage to find out anything specific about what had happened in the village of Miletici. They said they had problems in finding out all the details about the individuals who had committed those murders.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, if I have understood you correctly, although our units and the army didn't have this duty, you know that the 306th did want to find out what had happened there, but it was not possible for this unit to do so; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to what was possible to do, was it possible for them to enter the Mujahedin headquarters and investigate there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that there was a Mujahedin camp at the time. I don't know which methods the 306th used in order to obtain information, but I do know that they weren't able to obtain any information about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, let's now have a look at document under number 14, which is the Main Staff of the HVO, dated the 15th of May, 1993. It's from the Main Staff of the HVO. Earlier on, in response to a question of mine, you said that each event was reported in different ways, certain elements were added to the reports, but you mentioned what you found out when you spoke to the inhabitants and when you visited Miletici with the joint commission. It says the Travnik sector in this document, in the middle, it says the commander of all the 18 Muslim villages is Nihad Puric, a.k.a. Hadzija. "We have learned from a captured MOS member that the massacre in the village of Miletici was approved by the Italian commander Bahrudin Kumoro [phoen] and that the extremists were led by Senad Lukovic, together with Jasmin Jasarevic and Osman Tahirovic. Besides the Mujahedin the following men took part," et cetera, et cetera. Given the information you had, did the information you have prove in any way that what is claimed here is true?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to all the information I had, what is stated here is not correct; it's false. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In line -- on page 27, line 4, it says that the Mujahedin had some sort of command. But we were speaking about a camp. I didn't mention a Mujahedin command. I asked whether they entered the Mujahedin camp. And the general said that he wasn't even aware of the existence of such a camp at the time. So could that be corrected, please. Did anyone from the HVO -- I apologise. This document was P561, for the sake of the transcript. Did anyone from the international community, or did anyone else inform you that the BH army might have something to do with the events in Miletici?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout that period, did you remain a member of the joint commission which was also composed of members of the international community? And if that was the case, did they have the opportunity of drawing your attention to this matter?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The representatives of the international community did have this opportunity, and at meetings of the joint commission, they tried to clarify anything that wasn't clear. But I don't remember that at meetings of this joint commission which were held in Vitez up until May, in that year, which is when the joint command was formed in Travnik, as I said, I can't remember that members of the international community mentioned the problem of Miletici at one of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, when you look back to those events now, are you convinced that what happened, are you convinced that the crimes in Miletici had nothing to do with the army, and are you convinced that there's no doubt as to who had committed the crimes in Miletici?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I have already mentioned what I was aware of on that day, or rather, a day later, on the 25th of April, 1993, and given what I have seen here, I'm convinced that BH army members had nothing to do with those crimes. And similarly, in 1993, I was also convinced of this fact, after Franjo Nakic and I had obtained certain information. So I'm still convinced that the BH army had nothing to do with the murders committed in Miletici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would now like to provide the Chamber and my colleagues and the witness with a new series of documents that I will use to put questions to the witness about Maline. Perhaps we could then have a break and I'll then continue with my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You want to give him the binder and then he can have a look at it during the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will show the witness the binder, then. General, Defence counsel has provided you with some documents, a set of military documents. You'll have some time to have a look at the documents during the break and your examination will then continue. We will resume at about 5 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll now resume. You may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, on the first day when you were speaking about events in 1993, and in particular, about military events, you said that at the beginning of June, in Travnik, there was an HVO attack, and this then spread to the Bila valley. And you in the command received information on the difficult situation that the 306th Brigade was in. It had been completely cut off in that area. General, could you please tell me: As a member of the joint command in Travnik, in the course of May and at the beginning of June, did you go to Zenica, or rather, to Travnik? And how did you travel at the time?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: While the joint command operated in Travnik, I spent quite a lot of time in the Travnik area. Occasionally I would go to Zenica. When I went to Zenica, I would go with UNPROFOR vehicles and personnel carriers, because it wasn't possible to reach Zenica in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, you also said that in the course of the attack on Travnik at the beginning of June, you were in Travnik. Where were you on the 8th of June, 1993? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning of June I was in Travnik, in the joint command, and on the 8th of May, if I remember this correctly, I was in Zenica. I was in Zenica, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you have already said that you would obtain --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a mistake, or perhaps you were mistaken. So I won't correct this. You said on the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was a slip of the tongue. It wasn't on the 8th of May. On the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have told us about the news that you reached us [as interpreted] from the 306th Brigade and their requests for assistance. Tell me: Did the 3rd Corps decide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking at the transcript, and I'm totally lost. We don't know where we are. General, can you please tell us: The 8th of June, where were you? Were you in Zenica or were you in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 8th of June I was in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Now I'm clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, do you know if the 3rd Corps command decided to respond to the request of the 306th Brigade for assistance? Did the BiH army units from Zenica launch an attack from -- towards the Bila valley?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained the situation in Travnik in great detail. At the beginning of June, a few days after the fighting was over in Travnik, this fighting spread towards the area of Bila region, that is, around the Bila River. According to our information, the 306th Brigade was in a very difficult position. I've already explained why. They did ask for assistance. This request was so strong that the brigade commander was under the impression that he had come under attack from all sides, that he had come under a simultaneous attack by the HVO and the aggressor. We had different variations how we were going to use our units in case of attack, either by one enemy or the other, or both. At the time, the 306th was in a very difficult situation for quite a long time, so it was decided to use some of the 3rd Corps units in order to help the 306th Brigade. One part of the 3rd Corps units were indeed used from the direction of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, on that day -- strike that. Did these units that were moving from the direction of Zenica, did they achieve any military results? And if they did, in what area was that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main direction of action of the units from Zenica was via the Ovnak pass. Those were the units that went to assist the 306th Brigade. In the morning hours I received information that the units of the BiH army had some successes at the Ovnak pass, that they took control over this pass and that they were moving forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before I move on, please tell us: What happened at the Ovnak pass? Where were the strongest forces of the HVO with regard to the town of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ovnak pass had tactical importance. Whoever was in control of Ovnak had very good tactical positions. The HVO was there on Ovnak. The HVO was very strong there. That's why there was very fierce fighting there at the moment when the BiH army units launched an attack in order to take that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Once you learnt that our forces achieved some military results and that they managed to break through the strongest forces of the HVO in Ovnak, did you go there in order to inspect the military situation?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went to check the information that I had received. I arrived at Ovnak sometime around noon. I saw that Ovnak had been liberated, that our units were there, and that combat operations were moved to the west of Ovnak. In other words, the area of Ovnak was liberated. I moved even further. I don't know how far I moved into the Bila valley. However, I had to return to Zenica because of my previous very important commitments that I had in Zenica. Those commitments were to take place around 2.00 or 3.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, on that day, the 8th of June, or did -- any other subsequent days, did you learn that during the combat operations that had taken place on the 8th of June, some HVO prisoners or civilian prisoners were killed in the area of Ovnak or the Bila valley?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, the combat operations were still going on and were very intense. According to my initial information, the fighting was still on, and there were casualties on both sides, on the side of the HVO, as well as on the side of the BiH army. I did not have any information about murders having taken place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, did you subsequently learn that some murders or killings might have taken place on the 8th of June, during these combat operations? And if you did, who did you learn that from?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Due to the very complex situation that prevailed from the 8th of June, 1993 onwards, and the incidents that had already taken place in the area of Kakanj, to which I have already testified here, and due to the fact that there were already incidents in Zepce, and due to the overall situation that could be felt in Zepce after that, my entire attention, as well as the attention of the corps command, shifted from the Bila valley to the area of Kakanj, and subsequently to the area of Zepce. I did not have any information that murders or killings had taken place in the area of the Bila valley. The first information about the murders reached me from the international community. And as ever, as always before that, I reacted immediately. I suggested that we should go there in order to investigate what kind of murders or killings had taken place and were reported to us by the international community.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us when this happened, and can you tell us whether your suggestion was accepted? If it was, who was it who went to the area to inspect?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all of my previous activities and in all of the subsequent activities, whenever we received information from the international community that something had happened in the area controlled by the BiH army, I would immediately call for an investigation. I believe that this was in early August 1993 that we went there. Mr. Landry Remi represented the European monitors, Stjepan Radic also had expressed a desire to inspect the area where the combat activities had taken place, Stjepan Radic, who was a priest.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, did this delegation involving Mr. Remi and Mr. Radic did they go to the site? Where did you go and what did you learn there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the representatives of the European Monitoring Mission and Father Stjepan expressed a desire to visit the monastery in Guca Gora, this is where we arrived first. We inspected the situation around the monastery in Guca Gora. At the proposal of the European Monitoring Mission that we should go towards the village of Maline, I suggested that some of the soldiers should go with us, namely, the military police was already in Guca Gora, and we were given a soldier who escorted us towards the village of Maline. That was a soldier who could have provided us with some more information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, since Father Stjepan and the representative of the European Monitoring Mission wanted to inspect the monastery in Guca Gora, when you arrived at the monastery, was the monastery destroyed or were there any visible damages on the building of the monastery?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the monastery was not destroyed. However, there was some visible damage. On the walls there was some fresh paint, and there was some other damages, but it wasn't destroyed; that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Father Stjepan comment on the condition of the monastery and the fact that it was being secured by the military police of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember what Father Radic was saying at the time; however, I could see that he was quite satisfied with the fact that the monastery enjoyed protection by the military police, which meant that any further destruction would be prevented. And I could see that Father Radic was quite pleased with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said the international community expressed a desire to go to Maline and that one soldier was your escort, a soldier who hailed from that area. Tell me: Did you go to Maline? What did you see there? What did you learn there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A soldier escorted us to Maline, and he told us that there were two graveyards there where members of the HVO were buried after the combat operations that had taken place in the area. We asked him to show us the exact points where these graves were, and we inspected those sites. I would just like to mention that Father Radic had information that the monastery in Guca Gora had been completely demolished. That's why Father Radic was quite pleased with the situation that he found in Guca Gora. This is something I forgot to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The representatives of the international community, or Father Radic, or you personally, did you ask for additional information from the soldier who had shown you the places where the fallen members of the HVO had been buried?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I asked the soldier how this had happened and how come that members of the HVO had been buried in those two graves. The soldier told us that they -- their bodies were gathered after the clean-up of the area. He was not sure of their numbers. He said that there were only two graves and that there were no other graves in the area. I don't know what the others asked the soldier. I remember that Mr. Remi also put some questions to the soldier, as well as Father Radic, but I can't remember what they asked him. I only know what my questions to him were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, can you please look at document number 1 in the Maline set. On page 1, you can see under "general situation" that you and Father Radic from the church in Zenica were in Maline together with the representatives of the international community. This is exactly what you have just told us.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I can see here that this was on the 3rd of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the item 4B, can you read it, and can you tell us whether this is what you remember as to what happened and what you were talking about when you visited the monastery in Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is precisely so, but I didn't know that Mr. Radic said Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that I was very cooperative in the protection of religious facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Under C and D -- actually, only under C, you can see the description of your arrival in Maline or, in other words, in the area where the two graves were. According to the best of your recollection, what happened then, and is this report a true reflection of what happened and the conversations that took place at the time?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I've just told you that I don't know what Father Radic said or asked at the time, but I can see here that there were both soldiers and civilians buried in those two graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The number of this document is P164. General, was this the first information about what might have transpired on the 8th of June in the area of Maline?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that my -- according to my information, there had been combat operations, but not killings or murders. However, Father Radic and the representatives of the international community insisted, and what the soldier told us at the moment confirmed my information, the information that I had before I came to the site.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, you were telling us about the general situation which prevailed from mid-June to up to this period. Tell us: In view of the events in Zepce, where did you and the 3rd Corps commander spend your time? Where were you located at the time in order to be able to deal with the burning problems in Zepce?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already testified that we received an order sometime in mid-June to try and lift the blockade from Maglaj. The 3rd Corps commander, General Hadzihasanovic, decided to move his command post towards Zepce. We established the forward command post in a place called Postojna, in the municipality of Zepce. We invested all of our mental and physical efforts into lifting the blockade from Maglaj. Regardless of the fact that the combat operations were still going on in Central Bosnia, the corps commander, General Hadzihasanovic, decided to use all the available forces under the command of the 3rd Corps and channel them towards Maglaj, with a view to lifting the blockade from Maglaj. I spoke about that two days ago, in somewhat greater length. I told you about the situation that prevailed in the 3rd Corps at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, did there come a time when you had to deal with the issues raised before the 3rd Corps with regard to the developments that had taken place in Maline on the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that whenever the corps command received information of that sort, they would undertake appropriate measures. I remember that we received an order to draft a report on the events in Maline. This was in October 1993, and the letter was addressed to us from the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at documents 2 and 3. Is any of these two the document that you have just mentioned? The documents are P170 and P171.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen these documents before. Actually, I only saw the document that had arrived from the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did the 3rd Corps command do? What information did they receive, and what was your role in all that?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, within the system of control and command, when we learned that there was some additional information, we reacted immediately by asking the subordinate unit in that area to report to us as to what had happened in Maline.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the document number 4, which bears the number P111.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is precisely what I have just testified about. The command of the Bosanska Krajina G is requested to provide information about the events in Maline.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who signed this document on behalf of the commander?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am familiar with my commander's signature, this is not his signature. Somebody signed on his behalf. But I don't know who it was. In any case, this is not my signature and this is not my commander's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, did there come a time when you received an answer from your subordinate unit, an answer to your request to inform you what happened on the 8th of June, in Maline, during the combat operations there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A report arrived in the corps command. It arrived from the subordinate unit. And based on this report, I prepared my report for my superior command and the Supreme Command Staff. I prepared that report. I don't know where General Hadzihasanovic was at the time. So I decided to draft this document that would be sent to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at document number 5. This is our number 1498. And tell me whether this is the reply that you received from your subordinate unit. And then look at document number 6 and tell us whether this is your report that was a follow-up.

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first document is the report sent to us by the subordinate unit, and the second document is the document that I drafted and signed in the month of August. I was in the area together with the monitoring mission, and Father Radic. That's why my report provided some more detail, and I answered all the questions put to us by the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The document under number 6 bears number P174. When you provided reply to these documents, save for the information that you received on the 3rd of August, that is, the information that you received and the report sent to you by the subordinate unit, did you have any precise information or reasonable grounds to suspect that the events had transpired in the way different than the one described in your report?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have any such information. I collected all my information in the field, and based on the report that was provided to me at the request of the Supreme Command Staff, who wanted to know exactly what had happened in Maline.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you that a number of HVO prisoners had been killed in Maline?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard such questions here at The Hague Tribunal. I don't know exactly in which case this was, in which case these developments and the possible murders in Maline were mentioned. I remember very well that on that occasion, before another Trial Chamber, I said what I know, and I believe that I said and described the events in the same way I have described them now. I did know that there had been combat operations, that there were casualties on both sides during these combat operations, and that during the subsequent clean-up of the area, the bodies of the fallen soldiers were gathered and buried in the two graves. This is what I have already once said before this Tribunal, but I don't know in which case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, during the combat operations, or at any other time, on the 8th and 9th of June, did you visit Guca Gora? At whose request did you do that, if you did? And with whom did you go there, if indeed such a visit had taken place?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, 1993, I did not visit Guca Gora. I was in Guca Gora on the 9th of June, 1993. On the 9th of June, 1993, I arrived in Guca Gora at the request of UNPROFOR. I was accompanied by the UNPROFOR. In other words, I was in the BritBat personnel carrier. We arrived in Guca Gora from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Guca Gora, what did you find there?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an officer from BritBat who received me before the -- in front of the church and took me into the church. That's where I saw a large group of civilians of various ages and there were both men and women there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you can remember, how many people were there in and around the church?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice any civilians around the church, apart from UNPROFOR members, but I could see that there were between two and three hundred people in the church. I can't be precise, but there were about two to three hundred people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Among those civilians, were there any HVO members, and did you recognise anyone?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, there were people of various ages, there were children, there were old people, and there were also men who were able-bodied. After having had a look at the civilians, I noticed a member of the HVO whose name was Tomislav Rajic. I knew him from before, because at the beginning of the war he was in the defence staff in Travnik. I remember him well because we were involved in a joint operation which involved liberating the Vlasic relay which had been taken by the Serbian aggressor. So I knew Tomislav Rajic very well, and I was sure that that was the person. He was wearing civilian clothes. He wasn't in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, did you speak to Mr. Rajic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke to Mr. Rajic, and he asked me to help, to ensure that the civilians were cared for, to ensure that they were taken to Vitez. And since he was an HVO soldier, he said he was surrendering, he said I could imprison him. I said I didn't want to imprison anyone. I told him he could go with his people. I told him he could go wherever he wanted to go. But I said that he wouldn't be imprisoned. I told him he wouldn't be a prisoner of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, on that day, with the help of UNPROFOR, were all those people taken from Guca Gora to Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the afternoon on that day, all the civilians and all the able-bodied men who were in the church got into the BritBat personnel carriers and they were driven to Bila, that is to say, to Vitez. Not a single civilian remained in the church on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, as far as the fighting is concerned, at the beginning of June, on the 8th and 9th of June, did the fighting result in lifting the blockade of the road linking Zenica and Travnik?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, 1993, well, I have already said that on that date, the road through Ovnak was unblocked, and since I was in the church on the 9th of June, I could see that that road could be used too, because fighting was to the south of the church on the 9th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, tell me: Without UNPROFOR's help, was it possible for you to get from Zenica to Travnik, regardless of the fact that there was fighting in the vicinity, to the south of that road?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 9th of June, it wasn't possible to get there by other means. The only means was personnel carrier, because there was fighting near that road. But after a few days of combat, that road became passable. But a little further to the west, there was a shorter road which was constantly under HVO fire, and it was necessary to pass that part of the road very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General: After that, did you pass through Guca Gora; and if so, do you remember any particular event that you would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to?

utterances.speaker: DZEMAL MERDAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A few days after the 9th of June, 1993, I passed through Guca Gora. I came from the direction of Zenica and passed through Guca Gora. I can't remember the exact date, but I remember an event exceptionally well, because I was very impressed by this event. When passing through Guca Gora, I was told that there were foreigners in the church who wanted to destroy the church. Given the position of the BH army, according to which no religious buildings should be destroyed or even damaged, I entered the church immediately to verify the information I had been given.
